name: Imogen Lisle
languages: Latin (and enough Scots Gaelic to be corrected by old men in Cape Breton)
equipment: Heavy coat: a long tweed walking coat with deep pockets, too warm for Cambridge and not warm enough for Penobscot Bay
Silver knife, a Georgian fruit knife with a mother-of-pearl handle that was her grandmother's, kept for cutting apples and, she says, nothing else
Pocket revolver (a little nickel-plated .32 her brother pressed on her before her first field trip to the Outer Banks), 5 loaded, in her satchel under the notebooks
An Edison field phonograph in a wooden case, a recording horn, and twelve blank wax cylinders packed in cotton wool
Two recorded cylinders: an old sailor at the Rockland Sailors' Snug Harbor singing two verses of 'The Carrow Bell' in a cracked tenor
Zebulon Lunt's letter of May 1924, in a careful sexton's hand, promising to sing her 'the whole of it' if she comes to Carrow
Four field notebooks, a box of pencils, a pocket knife for sharpening them, and a copy of a famous collection of English and Scottish ballads with her own pencilled notes in every margin
A box of candles, matches in a tin, and a small brass lantern
A letter of introduction from her professor 'to any clergyman or schoolmaster of the Maine coast'
features: Seen It in a Book (Educated origin: once per long rest, recalls one true and useful fact of history, science, law or a book without a check; advantage on Research checks in a library, archive or registry; reads old handwriting, Latin inscriptions and legal language without a check)

Old Lore (Occultist: once the party has seen a creature or clear sign of it, an action and an INT (Occult) check, DC 10 + its CR, recalls one of its rules the party has not yet learned, which the GM chooses and which is always true; once per creature per long rest. Advantage on Occult checks to perform a rite or set a ward, done in half the usual time)
The Right Things in the Bag (Occultist: once per scenario, when a rite or ward needs a common object she could plausibly have packed, a candle, a nail, red thread, chalk, a little bell, she has it)
Steeped in It (Occultist, 2nd level: advantage on fear checks against the sign of a horror, DC 10; whenever she or the party learn one of a creature's rules, she loses 1 Dread)
Tradition: Folklorist (Occultist, 3rd level: advantage on Persuasion checks with the old, and an interview with the oldest person in a place always yields one true clue toward a creature's rule)

Library Privileges (Student background: a graduate student on a Harvard ballad-collecting project; she can get into any academic library and many private ones, professors will see her, and people explain things to her in more detail than to anyone else)
traits: The Right Things in the Bag

personality.traits: I sing under my breath when I'm thinking, and I am nearly always thinking. I ask the question everyone at the table has been carefully not asking, and then I write the answer down. I am delighted by things that frighten other people, until about a minute afterwards.
personality.ideals: A song is a memory that a whole town keeps together. If you want to know what a place is ashamed of, listen to what it sings and what it stops singing halfway through.
personality.bonds: Zebulon Lunt, whom I never met, who wrote to me in May that he would sing me the whole ballad, and was dead in June. Professor Aldenburg's song collection, which needs a chapter on the Maine islands and has had nothing from me in two years. My brother Hal in Hartford, who thinks I should marry a nice lawyer.
personality.flaws: I want the song more than I should. I will push an old woman to sing me a verse she is crying over, and be sorry later. I do not quite believe that anything I am collecting could reach out of the notebook and touch me.

appearance: A tall, long-necked woman of thirty-one with untidy chestnut hair pinned up and coming down, a freckled face, grey eyes behind round tortoiseshell spectacles, ink on her second finger, and a good low singing voice. Tweed coat, sensible boots, a hat that has been sat on, a satchel, and a phonograph case she will not let anyone else carry.
backstory: Imogen Lisle grew up in a Hartford minister's house full of hymn books and was sent to Radcliffe to become a teacher, and instead became the only woman on a Harvard professor's project to collect the old ballads that English, Scots and Irish settlers brought to America and kept singing long after they had been forgotten at home. She has spent five summers in the field, in the Appalachians, on the Outer Banks, in Cape Breton and along the Maine coast, with a phonograph and a notebook, sitting in kitchens. Last winter, in the Sailors' Snug Harbor at Rockland, an old Carrow-born seaman sang her two verses of a ballad she had never heard, 'The Carrow Bell', about a church that went into the sea while its bell rang, and then stopped and would not go on, and said that only Zeb Lunt knew the rest. She wrote to the sexton of Carrow Island. In May, Zebulon Lunt wrote back: he was old and not well, but if she came in the summer he would sing her the whole of it, 'and you will understand why the last verse is not mine to give in a letter'. She could not get away until October. She learned on the Rockland wharf that Zeb Lunt died in June, and she has come anyway, because a man does not write a letter like that about nothing. (Her two verses: 'Oh, the sea came over Carrow Bar the night the Point went down, and the bell rang out from the meeting house to the lanterns on the town.' And: 'Ring her an answer, ring her by hand, when the moon is full or new; ring her an answer from the land, and she'll sleep the whole tide through.' She does not yet know the third and fourth verses exist.)
